description: Test your knowledge of PA RN2 | Renal Pathology II: Tubulointerstitial, Vascular & Neoplastic.

cards.text: What is acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and why is it clinically significant?
cards.answer: ATN is the most important cause of intrinsic AKI. It results from severe ischaemia or direct nephrotoxic injury to tubular epithelial cells, causing acute loss of tubular function and reversible GFR decline.

tip.tip: ATN = #1 intrinsic AKI cause; remember TUBULES are damaged, not glomeruli or vessels

cards.text: Name the four interdependent mechanisms by which ATN reduces GFR.
cards.answer: 1) Tubular cell injury/death (ATP depletion), 2) Tubular obstruction (muddy-brown casts), 3) Backleak (denuded basement membrane), 4) Afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.

tip.tip: Injury + Obstruction + Backleak + Vasoconstriction = GFR collapse

cards.text: Why are the S3 segment of the proximal tubule and medullary thick ascending limb especially vulnerable in ischaemic ATN?
cards.answer: These segments have high metabolic oxygen demand but low collateral blood supply, making them preferential targets during ischaemic injury.

tip.tip: S3 & mTAL = High energy demand + low O₂ reserve = ischaemic hotspots

cards.text: Where does nephrotoxic ATN concentrate injury and why?
cards.answer: Nephrotoxic ATN injures the entire proximal convoluted tubule because toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin) are actively transported and concentrated in proximal tubule cells.

tip.tip: Nephrotoxins = whole PCT affected (not just S3) due to active uptake and lysosomal accumulation

cards.text: What are 'muddy-brown casts' and why are they a morphological hallmark of ATN?
cards.answer: Muddy-brown casts consist of necrotic cell debris, Tamm-Horsfall protein, and myoglobin (in rhabdomyolysis). They physically obstruct tubular lumens and are the pathognomonic finding of ATN.

tip.tip: Muddy-brown = necrotic debris + THP ± myoglobin; this is ATN's calling card

cards.text: List the six major categories of tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) with one prototype condition for each.
cards.answer: 1) Ischaemic—ATN (shock/hypoperfusion), 2) Toxic—ATN (drugs/rhabdomyolysis), 3) Infective—pyelonephritis, 4) Immune/allergic—drug-induced TIN (NSAIDs, penicillins, PPIs), 5) Metabolic—urate/oxalate nephropathy, 6) Obstructive—hydronephrosis-related atrophy.

tip.tip: ITIOM + O: Ischaemic, Toxic, Infective, Immune, metabolic, Obstructive

cards.text: What is tubulorrhexis and which form of ATN is it characteristic of?
cards.answer: Tubulorrhexis is rupture of the tubular basement membrane. It occurs in severe ischaemic ATN but is notably ABSENT in nephrotoxic ATN, where the basement membrane remains intact despite necrosis.

tip.tip: Tubulorrhexis (TBM rupture) = ischaemic ATN only; nephrotoxic = TBM stays intact

cards.text: How does the pattern of tubular necrosis differ between ischaemic and nephrotoxic ATN on microscopy?
cards.answer: Ischaemic ATN shows patchy, skip-lesion necrosis (irregular gaps along tubules); nephrotoxic ATN shows diffuse, uniform necrosis confined to the proximal convoluted tubule.

tip.tip: Ischaemic = spotty/patchy pattern; Nephrotoxic = diffuse/uniform distribution
